newsitem.title: INDONESIA: General Motors says sales hit by Jakarta car rule.
newsitem.headline: General Motors says sales hit by Jakarta car rule.

text.p: The Indonesian unit of U.S. automobile giant General Motors said on Tuesday its sales this year had been hurt by uncertainty in the market caused by Indonesia's national car policy.

Terence Johnsson, sales director of PT General Motors Buana Indonesia (GMBI), said the car policy, which gives tax and tariff breaks to a car company controlled by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra, had also affected future investment plans in Indonesia.
"The national car policy has created uncertainty in the market, which has affected our sales," Johnsson told Reuters.
He said sales in 1996 were expected to touch 4,000 units, around 2,000 cars less than earlier projections. The GMBI plant in Indonesia began operations in January this year.
He said GMBI's flagship Opel Balzer, a five-door multi-purpose, 2,200 cc vehicle that uses 40 percent local parts, was expected to account for 3,200 of total sales.
PT Timor, Hutomo's joint-venture with Kia Motors of South Korea, was given special tax and tariff breaks by the government in January to produce the Timor sedan as the national car.
Under the agreement, the Timor car must use 60 percent local content within three years of starting production, but currently it was importing fully assembled cars from South Korea.
Japan, the United States and the European Union are currently fighting the policy at the World Trade Organisation (WTO). They say it contravenes free trade regulations.
Johnsson said GMBI was putting off planned capital injections because of the car policy. He did not give details.
"It (the policy) will continue to cause a problem as long as the overall playing field stays uneven," he said.
General Motors invested $110 million in its Indonesian assembly plant, which came on-line in January.
Johnsson said a slower than expected start-up of the plant had also affected sales this year.
"We did not reach full capacity until the end of June," he said, adding that was a month later than scheduled.
He said next year's sales were targeted at 8,000 units, 15-20 percent of which would be exported to South Africa, Namibia, Kenya and Southeast Asian countries.
